extracted.intended_audience: British public, policymakers, and educated readers concerned with the French Revolution and public finance (late 18th-century context)
extracted.subtask_description: A reflective political pamphlet/essay critiquing revolutionary finance, governance, and constitutional change; articulates normative standards for fiscal prudence, public credit, property, and the tempering of liberty with restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in valuation of confiscated property
rubrics_metrics.description: When confiscating or using ecclesiastical/landed property as security, the state must show an 'open and exact statement of the clear value of the property' including rent-rolls, inventories, gross value, management charges, and encumbrances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues the government ought to 'ascertain the gross value of the estate, the charges of its management and disposition, the encumbrances perpetual and temporary' and 'when that surplus... had been clearly ascertained and properly vested in the hands of trustees' to render a land-bank tolerable. Anti-pattern: issuing assignats before any valuation or inventory; holding out estate 'disengaged of all charges' without authenticating value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper money must be backed and convertible
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper currency should originate from real cash deposits and be instantly convertible into specie without loss; paper must be accepted by choice, not by coercion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'our paper is of value in commerce, because in law it is of none' and 'not one shilling of paper money... is received but of choice; that the whole has had its origin in cash actually deposited; and that it is convertible at pleasure, in an instant and without the smallest loss, into cash again.' Anti-patterns: forced acceptance of paper, issuing unbacked paper leading to depreciation and loss of credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repeated, unbacked emissions of paper (assignats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing successive tranches of paper currency to cover deficits undermines credit and causes depreciation; the cure of issuing more depreciated notes is no remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: initial sixteen millions sterling of assignats depreciated 5-7%; critics propose 'issue new assignats' as remedy for old depreciation. Author ridicules the practice: 'Are the old assignats depreciated at market? -- What is the remedy? Issue new assignats.' Presents this as metaphysic/arithmetic folly and a chief cause of financial ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute confiscation for sound revenue sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Confiscations and plunder of church or citizen property do not constitute a durable resource; they destroy settled revenue and public credit rather than enrich the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author: 'Never did a state, in any case, enrich itself by the confiscations of the citizens.' Confiscation seen as both unjust and politically/financially self-defeating; confiscated estates carry encumbrances and additional charges that often exceed income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to make good pledges and to account for charges
rubrics_metrics.description: When the state pledges that confiscated estates will be 'disengaged of all charges' it must actually provide the accounting to support that pledge before issuing securities based on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to the 14 April 1790 resolution promising to account for expenses of religion etc.; author demands rent-rolls, inventories, and explicit statements of charges before emission of paper. Anti-pattern: issuing sixteen millions sterling immediately 'upon the credit of so handsome a declaration' without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for establishing a land-bank
rubrics_metrics.description: A land-bank should proceed like business: determine net surplus after charges, vest it in trustees, indicate parcels, times and conditions of sale, and permit creditors or purchasers to subscribe or purchase with full knowledge of what they buy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance lays out step-by-step: ascertain gross value and encumbrances, strike net surplus, vest security with trustees, specify parcels/time/conditions, admit public creditor to subscribe or receive proposals. Anti-patterns: obscure statements, hidden charges, no trustee vesting, driving buyers 'blindfolded'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve public credit by protecting settled revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not destroy the settled revenue of the state (the 'sole security for the public credit'); use transparent, lawful means to maintain revenue streams rather than temporary artifices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author condemns 'destroying the settled revenue of the state' to rebuild credit on confiscated property. Emphasizes that public credit rests on predictable revenue and lawful security, not on forced or fraudulent devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal prudence requires honest accounting of new expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of economy must be measured against the full set of new expenditures (Assembly, municipalities, armies, police, judicatures, pensions); reductions in some areas do not justify overall greater charge if new costs exceed receipts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author questions those who claim economy: 'Have those who say so looked at the expenses of the National Assembly itself... of the increased pay of the two armies...?' Warns that the present system may be 'beyond all comparison more chargeable' despite rhetoric of frugality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit must be earned in markets of commerce and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign and domestic lenders will not deal with a government that alters the nature of obligations by force or refuses lawful remedies; demonstrated solvency and respect for contracts attract capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author asks why Holland, Hamburg, Switzerland, Genoa, England would deal in paper for a people 'who attempt to reverse the very nature of things' and 'discharging one of his engagements with another.' Good credit requires legal stability and respect for obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coercion in financial measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Using force (bayonet) to impose monetary instruments or reverse obligations undermines moral and commercial confidence and renders financial contrivances ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly criticizes 'the debtor prescribing at the point of the bayonet the medium of his solvency to the creditor' and 'drag[ging] by the point of the bayonets their slaves... to take their fictions for currencies.' Financial instruments must be voluntary and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reforms should aim to preserve valuable institutions and property
rubrics_metrics.description: When altering constitution or laws, prefer preservation and repair in the style of existing institutions rather than wholesale destruction; changes should be guided by caution rooted in acknowledgment of human fallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author: 'I would make the reparation as nearly as possible in the style of the building... Let us imitate their caution if we wish to deserve their fortune...' Encourages conservative, measured reform rather than radical upheaval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom must be tempered by wisdom and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty without wisdom and virtue is dangerous; forming a free government requires balancing liberty and restraint via sagacious, combining minds, not mere declamations or popular bidding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line: 'What is liberty without wisdom and without virtue? It is the greatest of all possible evils.' Good government requires 'to temper together these opposite elements of liberty and restraint in one consistent work.' Anti-pattern: leaders outbidding each other with more 'splendidly popular' measures, stigmatizing moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must avoid pandering to popularity at the expense of sound policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Political leaders who bid for popularity risk becoming flatterers not legislators; moderation and compromise are necessary to preserve state stability even if unpopular in the short term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author warns that a leader proposing soberly limited liberty 'will be immediately outbid' and that 'Moderation will be stigmatized as the virtue of cowards.' The political consequence of pandering is long-term institutional damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject metaphysical or fanciful financial inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on fanciful schemes (coin church bells, magical remedies from plunder, alchemical fixes) as substitutes for sound economic measures; these are 'folies' that baffle argument and produce disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the project to coin church bells, the 'philosophic financiers' faith in church plunder, and comparison to Mr. Law's Mississippi scheme. Author recommends sober, tested commercial measures over 'metaphysic arithmeticians' and 'old, exploded contrivances of mercantile fraud.'
